The final answer is incorrect. The correct maximum is strictly less than 2^{999}.

**Why 2^{999} is not achievable:** Any intersecting family contains at most one set from each complementary pair {A, S∖A}, so |P| ≤ 2^{999}. But consider a transversal T, which contains exactly one element from each pair {i, 1001−i}. Then σ(T) = S∖T, so T and σ(T) are disjoint. Condition 3 forces σ(T) ∈ P whenever T ∈ P, which violates condition 2. So no transversal can be in P. Transversals come in 2^{500}/2 = 2^{499} complementary pairs, each contributing 0 instead of 1 to the count, so

|P| ≤ 2^{999} − 2^{499} < 2^{999}.

The same obstruction appears in small cases. For n = 2 the maximum is 1, not 2^1 = 2. For n = 4 the maximum is 6, not 8.

The proposed construction (sets with more than 500 elements) is also not reflection-closed in the required sense, and the claim that "the maximum is known to be 2^{n−1}" is unsupported. The number given as the final answer is 2^{999} itself, which is the trivial upper bound.

VERDICT: REJECT
CONFIDENCE: 5
